answer.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-mechanics problems (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%), and the inherited record points most directly at onboarding friction (memory_86, memory_31) as a lever with durable rather than one-off effects. That fits the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue better than the pricing response, which is the most emotionally urgent option but the least trustworthy evidence: memory_73 self-flags that its readout pooled two cohorts after a mid-test redefinition, so its 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' may be an artifact, and discount-led acquisition of price-sensitive SMBs is exactly the cohort most likely to churn or arrive as low-quality revenue. That is why memory_73 is my first verification pull: if the source record shows the confound was minor and the lift held per-cohort, promotional pricing becomes a live contender against the competitor; if not, I can stop treating it as evidence at all. Second pull is memory_86, because it is the direct load-bearing claim for my intended action and I want to know its population and horizon \u2014 whether the completion lift actually propagated to activation and retained revenue, or only to a completion metric, and whether it was measured on self-serve accounts comparable to today's mix. Activation messaging (memory_91) is my fallback if memory_86 turns out to be thin, since it targets the activation drop directly. Risks I am carrying forward rather than resolving: (1) cutting signup fields can degrade lead qualification and routing data, which could raise raw activation while lowering *qualified* revenue \u2014 so I will instrument qualified-pipeline and downstream conversion, not just first-week activation; (2) memory_44 says enterprise converts better sales-assisted, so any simplification must be scoped to the self-serve SMB path and must not strip the demo-request route; (3) all these memories are 15\u201364 days old and the competitive environment changed after them, so their effect sizes are priors, not forecasts. Standard experiment scale with a holdout and a segment guardrail, not a broad rollout, because the evidence supports direction more confidently than magnitude. Choosing onboarding does not close the pricing question \u2014 it defers it pending a clean readout.
